_doc: The guide's hierarchy: group > category > topic > article. Every article appears in exactly one topic. Entries starting with '@' are cross-references to an article that lives elsewhere (shown with an arrow, not counted as membership). 'start' is pinned as 'Start here' and must be one of the category's own articles. Urgent tiles and links point at a:article, f:flow, c:category or a route (#/...).

groups.title: Stay alive
groups.intro: The basics that keep you alive, in the order they usually matter: deal with injuries, get out of the cold and wet, then water, fire and food. Keep your head throughout.

categories.title: First aid
categories.intro: Life threats first: danger, response, breathing, bleeding. Then injuries and illness. Aligned with NHS, St John Ambulance and Resuscitation Council UK guidance.

categories.title: Shelter & warmth
categories.short: Out of the wind and wet
categories.intro: In Britain the cold and wet kill more people than anything else outdoors. Get out of the wind, off the ground and into dry layers before you do anything else.

categories.title: Water
categories.intro: You can last about three days without water, less in heat or hard work. Almost all UK water needs boiling before you drink it.

categories.title: Fire
categories.intro: Fire gives warmth, safe water, cooked food, light, morale and a signal. Get the essentials right first; the techniques are in Skills > Fire craft.

categories.title: Food
categories.intro: Food matters less than warmth and water in the first days, and wild food carries real risks. Learn the rules before you eat anything.

categories.title: Health & hygiene
categories.intro: Small problems become big ones when you can't get help. Clean hands, safe water, dry feet and early care for minor illness keep you going.

categories.title: Mindset
categories.intro: What you do in the first minutes, and how you keep your head over hours and days, matters as much as any skill. Start with STOP.

groups.title: Situations
groups.short: Lost, stranded, flood, storm, grid down
groups.intro: What to do in specific emergencies, from being lost on a hill to a power cut at home. Each starts with the most important actions.

categories.title: Lost in the hills or forest
categories.short: Stop, get found, or walk out
categories.intro: Most lost walkers are found quickly if they stop, stay warm and make themselves easy to see. Start with the first actions below.

categories.title: Stranded in a car in snow
categories.intro: A car is a shelter, a landmark and easy to find. Leaving it in a snowstorm is how people die.

categories.title: Injured and alone
categories.intro: Treat what you can, get warm, then decide whether you can move. Nobody knows you're hurt until you're missed, so plan for a long wait.

categories.title: Cold-water immersion
categories.intro: Sudden cold water makes you gasp and panic. Fight your instinct to swim hard: float for a minute or two until your breathing settles.

categories.title: Coast and tidal cut-off
categories.intro: British tides rise fast and big. Know the tide times before you go, and never try to swim round a headland.

categories.title: Flood
categories.short: Get high, stay out of it
categories.intro: Moving water is far stronger than it looks: 15 cm can knock you over and 60 cm can float a car. Get to high ground and stay out of flood water.

categories.title: Storms and severe weather
categories.intro: Most storm deaths in the UK come from falling trees, flying debris, flooding and cold. Get to shelter early and stay there.

categories.title: Heatwave
categories.intro: UK heatwaves kill thousands, mostly older people indoors. Keep cool, drink, and check on others.

categories.title: Fire and smoke
categories.intro: Moorland and forest fires move fast in wind. Smoke kills more people than flames. Get out early, upwind or downhill, and stay low.

categories.title: Power or grid down at home
categories.intro: A long power cut or supply failure at home: keep water, warmth, food and sanitation going, and work with your neighbours.

categories.title: Chemical or radiation incident
categories.short: Go in, stay in, tune in
categories.intro: If there's a chemical, radiation or major smoke release, the UK advice is simple: go in, stay in, tune in. Get inside, close up, and listen to the radio.

categories.title: Urban survival
categories.intro: Towns have more resources and more hazards: water in odd places, shelter everywhere, but crowds, traffic and broken infrastructure.

categories.title: Leave or shelter in place?
categories.intro: Staying put is usually safer than leaving. Know what would make you go, where you would go, and what you'd take.

groups.title: When help isn't coming
groups.intro: When nobody knows where you are, or help can't reach you: getting yourself out, getting through days and weeks, living off-grid, and treating injuries yourself.

categories.title: Self-rescue and walking out
categories.short: Stay or go, then walk out
categories.intro: Deciding whether to stay or go is the biggest decision you'll make. If you go, follow water and linear features downhill, pace yourself, and never take a risk you don't have to.

categories.title: Surviving days to weeks
categories.intro: Once you're past the first night, survival is about routine: water, fire, shelter maintenance, food, rest and hygiene, every day.

categories.title: Long-term off-grid
categories.intro: Living for weeks or months without supplies: a sustainable camp, permanent water and fire, food through the seasons, and making what you need.

categories.title: Medicine without help
categories.intro: When nobody can take over: how to keep wounds clean, splints working, fevers and dehydration under control, and someone who can't be moved alive.

groups.title: Skills
groups.intro: Techniques to practise before you need them.

categories.title: Navigation
categories.intro: Map and compass, grid references, finding north without a compass, and using this phone's compass, GPS and map.

categories.title: Knots & cordage
categories.intro: Six knots cover almost everything: shelters, loads, joining lines and climbing a rope. Plus making cordage from plants.

categories.title: Tools & repairs
categories.intro: Look after your knife, make what you're missing, and repair clothing, kit and electronics.

categories.title: Fire craft
categories.intro: Every way to light a fire with your kit, the best UK tinders, and how to build and carry a fire.

categories.title: Shelter building
categories.intro: Natural and tarp shelters, step by step, and how to make them stand up to British wind, rain and snow.

categories.title: Trapping & fishing
categories.intro: Most trapping is illegal or restricted in the UK, and fishing needs a licence or permission. Here is what the law allows, and what actually works.

categories.title: Cooking & preserving
categories.intro: Cooking safely on a fire, preparing wild food, and preserving food by smoking and drying.

categories.title: Hygiene & sanitation
categories.intro: Most illness in camps comes from dirty hands and poor sanitation. These habits prevent it.

categories.title: Weather reading
categories.intro: Read UK weather from the sky, the wind and the feel of the air when you have no forecast.
